title: Earthquakes

draft.title: Earthquakes
card: Earth's crust is broken into huge slabs of rock that move very slowly. A fault is a crack in the crust where blocks of rock can move past each other.
The blocks can catch on each other instead of sliding. Stress builds up in the rock, much like a bent stick storing energy.
An earthquake happens when the stress becomes too great and the rock suddenly slips. The slip releases energy as shaking waves that travel through the ground.
The point underground where the rock first slips is the focus. The shaking is usually strongest at the surface close to the focus and weaker farther away.
draft.remember: Stress builds along a fault, then the rock slips and the ground shakes.

opts: Built-up stress in rock is suddenly released by a slip
Rock slowly slides along a fault without ever catching
Shaking waves create a crack in the crust, forming a fault
Hot rock rises to the surface and pushes the ground apart
a.why: Rock catches along a fault, stress builds, and then the rock suddenly slips and releases energy as shaking waves. The shaking waves are the result of the slip. They do not create the fault first, so the reversed option is wrong.
a.clue: Think of a bent stick that suddenly snaps back.

b.q: Two blocks of rock along a fault in Tasmania are stuck together while the crust keeps moving. What is happening to the rock?
opts: Stress is building up, and a sudden slip may follow
Energy is draining away, so shaking becomes less likely
The fault is closing up, so no earthquake can happen
Shaking waves are already spreading through the ground
b.why: While the blocks stay stuck and the crust keeps moving, stress builds up in the rock. A sudden slip later can release it as an earthquake. The waves only spread after the slip, so shaking is not already under way.
b.clue: Shaking only starts after the rock slips.

a.best: Built-up stress in rock is suddenly released by a slip

b.best: Stress is building up, and a sudden slip may follow
